Because every curve is already normalised so its fat peak is 1, the absolute gap has a direct meaning and needs no further scaling. It does not need to know which breast is which, so it is what a blind measurement would see. **NORMAL vs NORMAL** is the baseline: how different two healthy breasts of the same patient are. If a cancer is to be spotted blind, a CANCER/NORMAL pair has to differ by clearly more than that. From the usable scans, the CANCER breast is the higher in **`{python} rule_text(rule, "CANCER vs NORMAL")`** of CANCER/NORMAL patients, and the two breasts differ by a median of **`{python} median_difference(differences_rule, "CANCER vs NORMAL")`**. From the rejected, fatty scans it is the higher in only **`{python} rule_text(rejected_results, "CANCER vs NORMAL")`**, about what chance would give, and the breasts differ by **`{python} median_difference(differences_rejected, "CANCER vs NORMAL")`**, close to the **`{python} median_difference(differences_rejected, "NORMAL vs NORMAL")`** of two NORMAL breasts. Fatty scans cannot tell a CANCER breast from a NORMAL one; the information is in the water-rich scans. The NORMAL vs NORMAL baseline is thin, though: `{python} nn_rule[1]` patients have two NORMAL breasts with usable scans and `{python} nn_rejected[1]` with rejected scans. ## Usable and rejected scans by age {#sec-usable-and-rejected-scans-by-age} Breasts are averaged within each age band, separately for NORMAL, BENIGN and CANCER, twice: once using only the scans that pass the test (usable), and once using only the scans it rejects. one dot per patient." plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 7 fig, (density_ax, age_ax) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4.6)) for ax in (density_ax, age_ax): ax.set_box_aspect(1) width = 0.38 for offset, group, colour in ((-width / 2, "compared", USABLE_COLOUR), (width / 2, "left out", REJECTED_COLOUR)): shares = [100 * density_share[group][c] for c in DENSITY_ORDER] density_ax.bar(np.arange(len(DENSITY_ORDER)) + offset, shares, width=width, color=colour, alpha=0.75, label=f"{group} ({len(rule_groups[group])} patients)") for k, s in enumerate(shares): density_ax.text(k + offset, s + 1, f"{s:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=5.5) density_ax.set_xticks(range(len(DENSITY_ORDER))) density_ax.set_xticklabels(DENSITY_ORDER, fontsize=5.5, rotation=35, ha="right", rotation_mode="anchor") density_ax.set(ylabel="patients (%)", title="Breast density in the radiology reports", ylim=(0, 80)) density_ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y") density_ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6, loc="upper left") box_with_points(age_ax, [(0, group_ages["compared"], USABLE_COLOUR), (1, group_ages["left out"], REJECTED_COLOUR)], np.random.default_rng(2)) age_ax.set_xticks([0, 1]) age_ax.set_xticklabels([f"compared\n(n = {len(group_ages['compared'])})", f"left out\n(n = {len(group_ages['left out'])})"]) age_ax.set(ylabel="age (years)", title=f"Age (Mann-Whitney p = {age_p:.1g})") age_ax.grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y") fig.tight_layout() plt.show() plt.rcParams["font.size"] = 10 ``` The pattern is clear (@fig-who-left-out): **the rule leaves out the fatty breasts.** Radiologists describe a mostly fatty breast as having “scattered areas of fibroglandular density” (BI-RADS B); that is the main description for **`{python} pct(density_share["left out"]["B: scattered fibroglandular"])`** of the patients left out but only **`{python} pct(density_share["compared"]["B: scattered fibroglandular"])`** of those compared. The patients compared are mostly heterogeneously or extremely dense (BI-RADS C/D: `{python} pct(density_share["compared"]["C: heterogeneously dense"] + density_share["compared"]["D: extremely dense"])`, against `{python} pct(density_share["left out"]["C: heterogeneously dense"] + density_share["left out"]["D: extremely dense"])` of those left out). They are also younger, median **`{python} f"{np.median(group_ages['compared']):.0f}"`** against **`{python} f"{np.median(group_ages['left out']):.0f}"`** years, as expected since breasts become fattier with age. | Mentioned in the patient's records | Compared | Left out | p (Fisher) | |---|---|---|---| | `{python} list(term_rows)[0]` | `{python} pct(term_rows[list(term_rows)[0]][0])` | pct(term_rows[list(term_rows)[8]][1])` | `{python} f"{term_rows[list(term_rows)[8]][2]:.1g}"` | Patients who came in with a palpable lump, often younger women with dense breasts, are more often compared; routine screening patients lean towards being left out. Mastitis and family history make no clear difference. ::: {.callout-note title="What this means"} 1. **The rule is, in effect, a breast-density filter.** Its scan-by-scan water-peak check, which never sees the clinical records, keeps mostly BI-RADS C/D breasts and drops mostly B. This confirms from independent records that rejected scans come from fatty tissue, not from bad measurements. 2. **This is where it would be most useful.** Dense breasts are where mammography is weakest (the reports here repeatedly say density “may obscure small masses”), so a method that works in dense breasts would complement it. 3. **It narrows who the result applies to.** The CANCER vs NORMAL result of the rule holds for younger women with dense breasts; for the older, fattier group it currently says nothing. 4. **Age cannot bias the comparison itself**: both breasts of a patient have the same age, so age decides only *who* is compared, not which breast comes out higher. ::: ### Is it just the odds of hitting glandular tissue? ```{python} #| echo: false # each breast's scans: usable or not breast_scans = defaultdict(list) for nova, side, label, curve, height, centre in scan_records: if label in COHORTS: breast_scans[nova, side].append(usable(height, centre, WATER_MIN, CENTRE_MIN)) def hit_model(novas_here): """Per-scan chance p of a usable scan; the share of patients with both breasts usable, predicted if every scan were an independent try with chance p (1 − (1 − p)^k per breast of k scans) and observed; and the share of breasts with a mix of usable and rejected scans, predicted (1 − p^k − (1 − p)^k) and observed.""" sides = [breast_scans[n, s] for n in novas_here for s in ("LEFT", "RIGHT")] p = np.mean([u for scans_here in sides for u in scans_here]) both_predicted = np.mean([np.prod([1 - (1 - p) ** len(breast_scans[n, s]) for s in ("LEFT", "RIGHT")]) for n in novas_here]) both_observed = np.mean([all(any(breast_scans[n, s]) for s in ("LEFT", "RIGHT")) for n in novas_here]) mixed_predicted = np.mean([1 - p ** len(x) - (1 - p) ** len(x) for x in sides]) mixed_observed = np.mean([0 < sum(x) < len(x) for x in sides]) return dict(n=len(novas_here), p=p, both_predicted=both_predicted, both_observed=both_observed, mixed_predicted=mixed_predicted, mixed_observed=mixed_observed) by_density = {c: hit_model([n for n in scanned_both if patient_density.get(n, "not stated") == c]) for c in DENSITY_ORDER if any(patient_density.get(n, "not stated") == c for n in scanned_both)} def scan_hit_rate(novas_here): values = [u for n in novas_here for s in ("LEFT", "RIGHT") for u in breast_scans[n, s]] return (np.mean(values) if values else np.nan), len(novas_here) AGE_SPLIT = 50 by_age = {c: {band: scan_hit_rate([n for n in scanned_both if patient_density.get(n) == c and n in patient_age and (patient_age[n] < AGE_SPLIT) == (band == "younger")]) for band in ("younger", "older")} for c in ("B: scattered fibroglandular", "C: heterogeneously dense")} def density_row(c): m = by_density[c] return f"| {c} | {m['n']} | {m['p']:.0%} | {m['both_observed']:.0%} | {m['mixed_observed']:.0%} |" density_table = "\n".join(["| Density | Patients | Scans usable | Patients with both breasts usable | Breasts whose scans disagree |", "|---|---|---|---|---|"] + [density_row(c) for c in by_density]) age_table = "\n".join([f"| Density | Chance a scan is usable, age < {AGE_SPLIT} | age ≥ {AGE_SPLIT} |", "|---|---|---|"] + [f"| {c} | {by_age[c]['younger'][0]:.0%} ({by_age[c]['younger'][1]} patients) | " f"{by_age[c]['older'][0]:.0%} ({by_age[c]['older'][1]} patients) |" for c in by_age]) ``` A dense breast holds more glandular tissue, so a scan placed anywhere in it is more likely to pass through some. The table shows, for each density, how often a scan is usable, how often a patient ends up with both breasts usable, and how often a breast's scans disagree (some usable, some rejected): ```{python} #| echo: false #| output: asis print(density_table) ``` **Density sets the odds.** A single scan is usable in `{python} f"{by_density['B: scattered fibroglandular']['p']:.0%}"` of cases in mostly fatty (B) breasts and `{python} f"{by_density['D: extremely dense']['p']:.0%}"` in extremely dense (D) ones. That is why the rule leaves out the fatty breasts. **A breast's scans usually agree.** Most breasts give all usable or all rejected scans. If each scan were an independent coin flip, about `{python} f"{by_density['C: heterogeneously dense']['mixed_predicted']:.0%}"` of C breasts would have a mix; only `{python} f"{by_density['C: heterogeneously dense']['mixed_observed']:.0%}"` do. The scans are taken close together and sample the same region, so if a scan misses, moving to a clearly different spot should help more than repeating nearby. **Age matters even at the same density:** ```{python} #| echo: false #| output: asis print(age_table) ``` Within the same BI-RADS category, younger patients' scans are usable two to four times as often. Either BI-RADS, a coarse four-step scale, hides real differences in density, or glandular tissue itself holds less water with age (it involutes after menopause, with fewer cells and more collagen), so even a scan that does hit it may not show a water peak above the threshold. This data cannot separate the two, and the groups are small.
